full_judgment:
Syed Md Dastagir Hussain J: Rule was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why Article 6(Ga) of the Import Policy Order 2012-2015 (Annexure-F) published in Bangladesh Gazette dated 24-12-2012 is in violation of section 15(e) of the Customs Act, 1969, section 26 of the Trade Mark Act, 2009 and section 3(1) of the Imports and Exports (Control) Act, 1950 and the order as contained in Nothi No. 196/AP/section-7(A)/2014-2015/8052 dated 6-11-2014 (Annexure-G) should not be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect. 

 3. Mr Mainul Hosein, the learned advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner submits that the impugned order is without lawful authority and is of no legal effect as per Article 6(Ga) of the Import Policy Order 2012-2015 inasmuch as there is no registered proprietor of Dove and Vaseline brands in Singapore which is the country of export in the present case and as such there is no scope for obtaining certificate from registered proprietor as per requirement of Article 6(Ga) of the Import Policy Order, 2012-2015. Further he submits that the Article 6(Ga) of the Import Policy Order, 2012-2015 is ultra vires of the parent statute being the Imports and Exports (Control) Act, 1950 inasmuch as Article 6(Ga) of the Import Policy Order, 2012-2015 being subordinate Legislation cannot override or subvert the operation of the provision of the parent statute in this case section 15(e) of the Customs Act, 1969 and section 26 of the Trade Mark, 2009 requiring certificate of intellectual property right from proprietor of the exporting country for clearance of goods in Bangladesh even though section 15(c) requires only that the goods be manufactured outside of Bangladesh and the name of the place of manufacture be conspicuously displayed on the product in cases involving intellectual property in relation to import. Further he submits that the Article 6(Ga) of the Import Policy Order, 2012-2015 has not prohibited but only tried to regulate imported items in questions by requiring to obtain certificate from the proprietor and since no such proprietor is available in Singapore the same Article 6(Ga) is not applicable. Article 6(Ga) of the Import 2012-2015 is ultra vires to section 3(1) of the Import and Exports (Control) Act, 1950-2015 i.e. the delegating Act inasmuch as the delegating statute has not expressly authorised which are otherwise authorised by another statute namely section 15(e) of the Customs Act and, as such, Article 6(Ga) is also arbitrary, malafide, unreasonable and discriminatory by its operation in between different clauses of goods and involves subjective oppressive interference with the rights of the petitioner. The goods are lying after completion of customs assessment since almost last three months and the payment for the goods having been remitted outside of Bangladesh, the imported goods not being prohibited items may be released for ends of justice and equity. 

 4. Mr Samarendra Nath Biswas, the learned Assistant Attorney-General appearing, on behalf of the respondent No. 3 by filing affidavit-in-opposition submits that the provision of section 3(1) of the Imports and Exports (Control) Act, 1950 empowers the Government to prohibit or restrict imports and exports and exercising the power under the abovementioned section Government formulated the Import Policy Order, 2012-2015 which provides that if any brand products registered in Bangladesh under a law relating to intellectual property right is imported the certificate named intellectual property proprietor must be decided at the time of clearance of the goods from the Bangladesh Customs Authority. The said provision has been made in the Import Policy Order with a view to protect the import of any counterfeited goods and to protect the business right of the bonafide businessman and the consumers will be able to get the original products of the producer. In the instant case it appears that the petitioner though has imported the goods but it has not got the certificate as per the provision of law. Moreover a complain has been lodged by the respondent No. 7 regarding the consignment, the Customs authority has rightly and lawfully refused to release the goods imported by the petitioner. 

 5. Respondent No. 7 Unilever Bangladesh Limited being added as Respondent No. 7 contested the instant case by filing affidavit-in-opposition. Mr Rokonuddin Mahmood, the learned advocate appearing on behalf of the respondent No. 7 submits that the Customs Authority conducted 100 percent physical examination of the consignment in question, the consignment included goods which required certification under Article 5(6)(Ga) of the Import Policy Order 2012-2015 and accordingly issued the order dated 6-11-2014 (Annexure-G to the writ petition). The goods included in the consignment, which contained intellectual property owned by Unilever PLC and its affiliates may be released in favour of the writ petitioner only if the writ petitioner is able to obtain necessary certificate from Unilever PLC or its appropriate affiliates which the writ petitioner has not been able to obtain as such, the customs authority did not commit any wrong. Admitted position is that the respondent No. 7 lodged a complaint. The submitted certificate shows that Unilever Asia Private Limited Singapore is the licensee of the Dove and Vaseline brands in Singapore, and a copy of trade mark renewal certificate issued by the Assistant Registrar of Trade Marks for the Registrar, certifying that the flying dove was registered under class 3 of the Fourth Schedule of the Trade Marks Rules, 1963 in respect of symbol renewed in favour of Unilever PLC of England to the respondent No. 6. Further he submits that the purported importation of Unilever products by the petitioner is violative of section 3(1) of the Imports and Exports (Control) Act, 1950, because the Government of Bangladesh by Clause 5(6)(Ga) of the Import Policy Order, 2012-2015 prohibits import of any product in violation of intellectual property right without submission of certificate of the exporter having title in the trade mark in the country of export. The Customs Authority directed the petitioner to submit intellectual property proprietor's certificate as per Article 5(6)(Ga) of the Import Policy Order, 2012-2015. Therefore direction is lawful and the customs authority is under legal obligation to require intellectual property proprietor's certificate under section 3(2) of the Imports and Exports (Control) Act, 1950 read with Article 5(6)(Ga) of the Import Policy Order 2012-2015. Further he submits that section 15 of the Customs Act, 1969 is one of the provisions which regulate the import of goods and as such section 15 may not be read in isolation, rather should be read in conjunction with other relevant provisions, including sections 2(s) and 17 of the Customs Act, 1969. Therefore the import is in violation of the applicable laws of the Country. The Customs Authority requiring the petitioner to submit intellectual property proprietor's certificate in terms of Article 6(Ga) of the Import Policy Order 2012-2015 is not violative of petitioner's fundamental rights guaranteed under Articles 27, 31 and 40 of the Constitution. It is misconceived inasmuch as the Customs Authority is merely implementing the provisions of the law of the land as such the instant Rule is liable to be discharged with costs. The respondent No. 7 is the only authorized user of intellectual property including trade mark of the Unilever branded products in Bangladesh and, as such, the petitioner's purported importation is in violation of section 25(2) of the Trade Mark Act, 2009 and, as such, purported importation of Unilever branded products without permission is barred under section 3(2) of the Imports and exports (Control) Act, 1950 read with clause 5(6)(Ga) of the Import Policy Order, 2012-2015. 

 6. Heard the learned advocates, perused the application as it appears. The petitioner wanted to submit that the goods as imported are not fake, prohibited and restricted under section 3(1) of the Imports and Exports (Control) Act 1950. Therefore it cannot be regulated by section 5(6)(Ga) of the said Act as per delegated power and, as such, it is out of jurisdiction. Demand of the Customs Authority for obtaining certificate is thereby without jurisdiction. Moreso the certificate of intellectual property right cannot be issued from Singapore as Singapore is the licensee of Unilever brands and thereby Singapore has no authority to issue any certificate of intellectual property right. Section 6(Ga) of the Import Policy Order, 2012-2015 runs as follows:- 

 Therefore the customs authority was asking the petitioner to submit intellectual certificate from the country of origin within 7 days and that was under section 6(Ga) which is in accordance with law. From the reading of LC as per Annexure-A it appears that the name of address of beneficiary is HAI FOONG departmental store. Therefore the purchase is not from the owner of intellectual property right holder or country of origin. The customs authority asked to submit the certificate from the country of origin under section 6(Ga) of the Imports and Exports (Control) Act, 1950 therefore it is in accordance with law. The Customs authority has not committed any wrong asking for the certificate. Further as it appears from Annexure-D that Unilever Asia Private Limited of Singapore is the intellectual property right licensee and they have not sold the branded product to the petitioner. Therefore it reveals that the property as has been imported is not the branded product covered under the intellectual property right. Article 6(Ga) of the Import Policy Order 2012-2015 requires that if any branded product is imported under intellectual property Act, the certificate is to be produced from the country of origin at the time of release before the Customs Authority. Since the petitioner could not produce the certificate, the imported goods could not be released. Under such facts and circumstances we do not find any substance in this Rule.
